A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same AFRIDOC-MT corpus and benchmarking study. Their text, tables, figures, and appendices A–D are readable and support comparison despite substantial reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original translation benchmarks, fine-tuning experiments, GPT-4o evaluations, and analyses of model outputs.

after.justification: v2 retains the original benchmark experiments and reports additional human ratings, annotator agreement, and error analyses.

M1.justification: The translation procedures remain unchanged: fixed-size sentence chunking, document realignment, prompt augmentation, and supervised fine-tuning of NLLB-200, LLaMAX3, and Llama3.1. No new translation architecture, objective, or inference component is introduced.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same health and technology corpus, English and five African languages, and sentence/pseudo-document translation scenarios. The new human and judge evaluations assess outputs within this existing coverage; they introduce no new translation dataset or task.

E2.justification: The automatic benchmark comparator sets are unchanged. However, GPT-4o self-evaluation rows in v1 Tables 8 and 12 disappear from v2’s judge comparisons. The under-generation and off-target plots also replace LLaMAX3-Alpaca with LLaMAX3-SFT1.

E3.justification: v2 adds human direct assessment using error-span annotation and 0–100 ratings, describing 80 documents per annotator with 30 shared instances (Appendix B.7). It expands GPT-4o judging from three to five existing languages, adds a ModernBERT quality-estimation evaluation, and introduces an over-generation threshold of 143% of reference length. Existing training and decoding settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds native-speaker qualitative analysis of repetition, diacritics, and context preservation, plus explicit over-generation measurements (Section 5.5 and Figures 1 and 8). It also reports ModernBERT’s failure to distinguish model quality. Earlier document-length, prompt-sensitivity, repetition, and fine-tuning analyses are largely retained.

E5.justification: v2 introduces inter-annotator reliability assessment using Krippendorff’s alpha over 30 shared documents, reporting values of 0.40–0.81 (Appendix C.4). Both versions retain bootstrap resampling with 1,000 samples and 95% confidence intervals for automatic scores; no increased training-run or seed count is established.

E6.justification: All matched automatic benchmark table values are unchanged. v2 adds human DA results, expanded/revised GPT-4o judgments, over-generation rates, and absolute NLLB scores across 30 directions. For example, Table 10 newly reports Amharic DA scores of 64.5 versus 27.4 for LLaMAX3-SFT1 sentence versus pseudo-document translation. These are additional evaluations, not improvements over v1’s automatic benchmark scores.

T1.justification: Neither version develops theoretical results or proofs, and the pseudo-document construction is unchanged. The added scoring scales, length thresholds, and agreement measures concern empirical evaluation rather than new formal mathematical reasoning.

C1.justification: The dataset contribution and principal model rankings remain. However, v1 emphasizes GPT-4o judgments favoring pseudo-document fluency and accuracy, whereas v2’s introduction and conclusion question GPT-4o’s reliability for African-language evaluation and emphasize human evidence favoring sentence-by-sentence translation. The abstract also adds over-generation to the reported failure modes.

C2.justification: v2 moves beyond v1’s self-bias caveat to interpreting GPT-4o judgments as unreliable for African-language outputs. It adds explanations involving repetition and length generalization, discusses ModernBERT’s uninformative scores, and introduces explicit, unquantified limitations concerning translationese and English-source bias.

D1.justification: v2 changes the promised GitHub release to stated Hugging Face/GitHub data availability and specifies domain-specific licenses. It adds human-evaluation recruitment, compensation, annotation-framework details, and ModernBERT tokenizer statistics. The previously documented training hyperparameters, decoding limits, and translation prompts remain unchanged.

R1.justification: v2 adds targeted references on document chunking, length generalization, error-span annotation/Appraise, and translationese-related evaluation bias. These support the expanded evaluation and limitations discussion; the core positioning relative to African-language datasets and document-level MT remains substantially unchanged.

P1.justification: v2 substantially rewrites and condenses existing corpus, experimental, discussion, and conclusion prose. It moves quality-control and token-statistics explanations from Appendix A into the main text, removes duplicated discussion from Appendix D, and reorganizes the results and experimental appendices around human and qualitative evaluation.

P2.justification: v2 redesigns GPT-4o evaluation tables around individual languages, adds human-rating and annotation-allocation tables, combines error plots into a multipanel Figure 1, and adds absolute NLLB heatmaps. Corpus token statistics move into the main text, while existing fine-tuning difference heatmaps and prompt plots are retained elsewhere.

improvement.justification: Human ratings, agreement statistics, and qualitative analysis address v1’s reliance on GPT-4o judgments and provide useful evidence for revising the conclusions. Data-access and licensing disclosures also improve usability. However, v2 contradicts itself about recruiting Zulu annotators (Section 8 versus Appendix C.4 and the rating tables), and Section 5.3 misattributes the 4.9 fluency scores shown in Table 9. These reporting problems limit the overall gain.
